notes.title: Start here: a library tracker where one action touches several records
notes.body:
This repo is a Java 17 command-line library tracker: books, borrowers and loans, saved to a data directory. It looks small, but the course in astraupskill/ uses it to teach consistency: one librarian action has to keep several related records in agreement.

The code, in the order the codebase map suggests:

- **model/** - Book, Borrower and Loan (immutable values) plus Values (shared validation helpers).
- **storage/LibraryData** - the whole workspace as one record, with a constructor that validates it.
- **service/LibraryManager** - the business operations (add, edit, check out, return, delete, archive).
- **storage/FileStorage** - reading and writing the data files.
- **App** - the numbered menu; 01-CODEBASE-MAP has a table of every option and its prompts.

Read README, 01, 02, 03, 04 and 07 in astraupskill/. The 44 regression tests in test/librarytracker run with plain javac and java; 04 shows the commands.

excerpts.quote: one business action changes several related records
Each row lists the prompts in the order the CLI reads them

readMore.why: The CLI menu table maps each number to its prompts and service call.

notes.title: Core idea: the whole library is validated as one value
notes.body:
Each model class checks its own fields: a Book checks its title and its loan fields, a Loan checks its dates, Values checks text, emails, ids and date ranges. But some rules are about several records at once, and no single object can check them. Those live in the LibraryData constructor.

LibraryData holds a revision number, three id watermarks and the three lists. Its constructor runs every time the manager builds a new candidate state and every time a file is loaded, so a bad combination is refused whether it came from a command or from disk.

Read that constructor slowly and write each rule it enforces as one plain sentence. Then, for each rule, find which manager method could break it and the regression test that proves it is refused. Also find which manager methods enforce a rule themselves before LibraryData ever sees the candidate, and compare their messages.

excerpts.quote: [LibraryData](../src/librarytracker/storage/LibraryData.java) validates the aggregate.
public record LibraryData(

readMore.why: Chapter 02 explains why related records form a consistency boundary.

notes.title: Core idea: candidate, commit, and a second session
notes.body:
Every mutating method in LibraryManager ends the same way: it builds replacement lists and calls a private method, commit. commit creates a candidate LibraryData with the next revision and hands it to FileStorage.save. Trace commit and note the exact order of its statements.

FileStorage.save then does the file work under a cooperative lock and ends by replacing the snapshot file atomically. Read it and list every check it makes before it writes anything, and which fields it updates afterwards.

Two experiments make this concrete. First, read the test that injects a failure into the replacement step and list what it checks afterwards. Second, imagine two app windows open on the same directory. Write down what each one has in memory and on disk after the first one saves, then read the test about separate sessions to check your answer.

Startup also has rules: the file store reads library.snapshot if it exists, and otherwise looks at the two older text files.

notes.title: Why the first loan in a new workspace is loan 0
notes.body:
**Key: Loan 0, because an empty workspace starts all three id watermarks at 0.**

LibraryData.empty() builds the first state with revision 0 and nextBookId, nextBorrowerId and nextLoanId all 0. Each record type allocates from its own watermark, so the first book is 0, the first borrower is 0 and the first loan is 0. Values.identity accepts 0; it only rejects negative ids and Long.MAX_VALUE. Piping the three commands into the CLI prints "Book checked out and saved. Loan 0."

Why the others are wrong:
- **identity(id, 1) makes loans start at 1**: the 1 is a placeholder version so the id rule can be reused; 02-CONCEPTS warns that it is easy to misread.
- **Zero means "no loan"**: a book with no loan has a null borrowerId; ids do not reserve zero.
- **Loan 2 after book and borrower**: watermarks are per record type, not shared.

excerpts.quote: return new LibraryData(0, 0, 0, 0, List.of(), List.of(), List.of());
the first checkout in a new workspace prints `Loan 0.`

notes.title: Why loan history keeps the old title and name
notes.body:
**Key: history shows "Reliable systems" and "Sam Reader", the text accepted at checkout.**

checkOutBook builds the Loan with b.getTitle() and person.getName(), so the receipt holds its own copy of both strings next to the book and borrower ids. Editing a book or borrower replaces that Book or Borrower object; the Loan is never touched. Return uses loan.returned(date), which copies every field and only adds the return date. A probe that renames both records before returning prints the original text.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Looked up through the ids**: the history printer reads l.bookTitle() and l.borrowerName() from the receipt, not the current records.
- **Return rewrites the text**: returned() keeps bookTitle and borrowerName as they were.
- **Only ids**: Loan has bookTitle and borrowerName fields precisely so history stays understandable.

excerpts.quote: new Loan( data.nextLoanId(), bookId, borrowerId, b.getTitle(), person.getName(), at, due, null);
Renaming the profile preserves the reference while leaving the receipt text unchanged.

notes.title: Why checkout and return each bump the book version
notes.body:
**Key: version 3, because checkout and return each build a replacement with the next version.**

Book is immutable. checkOut returns a new Book built with Values.nextVersion(version), so version 1 becomes 2. returnBook does the same, so 2 becomes 3. The regression test quoted in 04 asserts returned.getVersion() == 3 and also that the old object still reports checked out, which proves nothing was mutated in place.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Only edits bump the version**: any replacement of the book does, because the version protects a librarian's view of the whole record, including its loan state.
- **Return restores version 2... or 1**: versions only move forward; there is no "restore".
- **Loan state lives only in the receipt**: the book itself carries checkedOut, borrowerId and dates, and LibraryData checks they agree with the active loan.

excerpts.quote: id, Values.nextVersion(version), title, author, isbn, true, true, borrower, at, due);
&& returned.getVersion() == 3);

notes.title: Why a borrower with an active loan cannot be archived
notes.body:
**Key: it is refused until the borrower's active loans have been returned.**

setBorrowerActive checks the version, then, when archiving, looks for any loan with that borrower id and no return date. One exists, so it throws "Return this borrower's active loans before archiving." The App prints it after "Change not accepted:". Even without this check, LibraryData refuses a state where an active loan belongs to an archived borrower.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Loan closed with today's date**: archiving never touches loans; only returnBook stamps a return date.
- **Book stays out to an archived borrower**: that is exactly the inconsistent state both the service and LibraryData refuse.
- **Book made available**: archiving a borrower does not change any book.

excerpts.quote: throw new IllegalStateException("Return this borrower's active loans before archiving.");
active loans block book and borrower archival

notes.title: Why a book with loan history cannot be deleted
notes.body:
**Key: "Change not accepted: Book has loan history. Archive it instead."**

deleteBook checks the version, then refuses if any loan refers to the book, whether that loan is active or returned. Deleting it would leave a receipt pointing at a record that no longer exists, and LibraryData would refuse such a loan reference anyway. Archival (option 17) retires the book while keeping history valid.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Book deleted and saved."**: only books with no loans at all can be deleted.
- **The borrower message**: that wording belongs to deleteBorrower; this is a book.
- **"Active loan missing."**: that message comes from returnBook when no active loan exists, not from delete.

excerpts.quote: if (data.loans().stream().anyMatch(l -> l.bookId() == id)) throw new IllegalStateException("Book has loan history. Archive it instead.");
Once history exists, deletion is rejected.

notes.title: How email normalization decides which registration collides
notes.body:
**Key: only the fourth is refused, because emails are lowercased and blank ones are stored as null.**

Values.email strips the text. A blank result becomes null; anything else must look like name@domain.tld and is lowercased with Locale.ROOT. LibraryData adds each non-null email to a set and throws "Borrower email is already registered." on a repeat. The first two are null, so they never collide. The third is stored as sam@x.org, and the fourth normalizes to the same value. A probe registering these four confirms it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The second (two empties)**: null emails are skipped by the uniqueness check; the test "blank optional emails may repeat" pins this.
- **None, exact comparison**: the comparison happens after lowercasing.
- **Capitals rejected**: capitals are accepted and normalized, not refused.

excerpts.quote: return clean == null ? null : clean.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
if (b.getEmail() != null && !emails.add(b.getEmail())) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Borrower email is already registered.");

notes.title: Why a failed save leaves no half-finished checkout
notes.body:
**Key: the book is still available and there is no new receipt, because data is assigned only after save.**

commit builds the candidate LibraryData (new book version plus the appended loan), calls storage.save(candidate), and only on the next line assigns data = candidate. When save throws, that assignment never happens, so every read still sees the previous accepted state. The regression test injects a throwing replacement step and checks the book, the loan list and the file bytes.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Written on the next save**: there is no pending queue; a rejected candidate is simply dropped.
- **Book out, no receipt**: book and loan are in one candidate and one file, so they are accepted or rejected together.
- **Empty library**: the old state is kept, not cleared.

excerpts.quote: storage.save(candidate); data = candidate;
If the manager assigned its candidate before saving, the terminal could show a checkout that disappears after restart.

notes.title: How a second session is stopped from overwriting the first
notes.body:
**Key: B is refused because the snapshot changed, and after a reload it can retry.**

Each FileStorage remembers the snapshot bytes it last read (baseline). In save, under the library.lock file lock, it compares the baseline with the current file. A's save changed the file, so B's comparison fails and save throws "Library changed in another session. Reload and review before retrying." Option 15 reloads, which refreshes B's data and baseline, and the retried registration succeeds. A probe shows exactly this sequence.

Why the others are wrong:
- **B saves and A's book is lost**: preventing that lost update is the purpose of the baseline check.
- **Changes merged**: there is no merge logic; the whole snapshot is replaced or the save is refused.
- **B waits on the lock**: A released the lock when its save finished; B gets the lock immediately and then fails the comparison.

excerpts.quote: if (!Arrays.equals(baseline, read(snapshotFile))
separate sessions reject stale files then recover by reload

notes.title: Which layer rejects a due date before the checkout date
notes.body:
**Key: "Change not accepted: Due date cannot precede checkout."**

checkOutBook takes today's date from the clock and calls old.checkOut(borrowerId, at, due) before it builds the Loan. Book.checkOut constructs a new Book, and the Book constructor throws "Due date cannot precede checkout." when the due date is earlier than the checkout date. The Loan constructor has a similar rule with different wording, but it is never reached. A probe with yesterday's date returns the Book message.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Due date precedes checkout."**: that is the Loan's message; the Book check runs first.
- **Checked out with the date moved to today**: nothing adjusts dates; invalid input is refused.
- **"Date must be within 1970..2100."**: yesterday is inside that range.

excerpts.quote: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Due date cannot precede checkout.");
Book b = old.checkOut(borrowerId, at, due);

notes.title: Why a deleted book id is never handed out again
notes.body:
**Key: the new book gets id 2, because nextBookId is a stored watermark that a delete never lowers.**

addBook creates the book with data.nextBookId() and commits nextBookId + 1. deleteBook commits the same watermark it had, so after deleting book 1 the watermark is still 2. The watermark is written into the snapshot, and FileStorage.save refuses any candidate whose watermark moves backward, so a restart cannot reuse 1 either. A probe shows the next book is 2.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Lowest unused id**: there is no gap search; allocation only reads the watermark.
- **Rebuilt from the highest present**: that is how some projects work, but here the watermark is persisted precisely to avoid it.
- **Restart at 0**: book 0 still exists, and LibraryData rejects an id that is not below the watermark.

excerpts.quote: data.nextBookId() + 1,
A durable next-ID watermark prevents reuse after deletion.

notes.title: Why a lone legacy file stops startup
notes.body:
**Key: startup stops with exit code 1, because both legacy files are required.**

With no library.snapshot, load reads books.txt and borrowers.txt. If exactly one exists it throws "Both legacy files are required; missing data is not an empty collection." main catches the IOException, prints "Startup stopped; existing library files were not replaced." with that message, and calls System.exit(1). Running the CLI on such a directory prints this and exits 1.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Books with an empty borrower list**: a missing file is treated as missing data, not as zero borrowers, because a checked-out book could point at a borrower that is gone.
- **Start empty and write a snapshot**: startup stops before the menu, so nothing is written.
- **borrowers.txt created later**: the app never writes the legacy files; it only creates library.snapshot.

excerpts.quote: if ((books == null) != (borrowers == null))
"Startup stopped; existing library files were not replaced. " + e.getMessage()); System.exit(1);

notes.title: Why a capitalized search status is refused
notes.body:
**Key: "Change not accepted: Invalid search or status."**

searchBooks accepts a status only if List.of("all", "available", "out", "archived").contains(status) is true. contains uses equals, which is case-sensitive, so "Available" fails and the method throws IllegalArgumentException. Every handler in App shares one catch that prints "Change not accepted: ", so even this read-only command gets that wording. Piped input prints exactly this line.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Case-folded to available**: only the query text is lowercased; the status is compared as typed.
- **"No matching books."**: that is printed for a valid search with no results, and this search is not valid.
- **Unknown status falls back to all**: an unknown status throws; it has no fallback.

excerpts.quote: !List.of("all", "available", "out", "archived").contains(status)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid search or status.");
System.out.println("Change not accepted: " + e.getMessage());

notes.title: Going further: the C# translation, the practice harness and the review checklists
notes.body:
The later questions use three more documents.

1. **astraupskill/08-TRANSLATION.md** is a short table: each row puts one design choice of this Java tracker next to its C# and EF Core equivalent. Read each row as "same rule, different mechanism" and ask what EF Core does for you and what you must still decide.
2. **astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md** grows the library toward a web service through five exercises, each with a Goal and a Check. Read the setup section and the shared helper first: how the checks are run explains a lot about how the exercises are written.
3. **docs/onboarding/02-review-checklists.md** gives one checklist per area of the code (services, CLI, persistence, models, side effects, security, errors, tests). The onboarding pages were written against an earlier, simpler version of the code (two text files, no Loan class), so use them for review habits and check every concrete fact against the current source.

excerpts.quote: Each exercise has a **Goal** and a **Check**.

notes.title: In EF Core the receipt is copied columns, not a join
notes.body:
A receipt must say what was true when the loan was made. In EF Core that means copying the title and the borrower's name onto the loan row (BookTitleAtLoan, BorrowerNameAtLoan) in the same SaveChanges that inserts the loan. A join to Books would always show today's title.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- A navigation property loaded with Include is exactly the join the course warns against; the duplicate text is the point, not a waste.
- No title-history column is proposed; the loan keeps its own copy.
- A view over the current tables would also show current values.

The course calls this the one thing to keep from the whole translation.

excerpts.quote: a join to `Books` would show the *current* title, which is the wrong answer for a receipt
In EF Core that is a plain column, not a navigation property.

notes.title: How EF Core turns a version check into a conditional UPDATE
notes.body:
Mark a property as a concurrency token ([Timestamp] byte[] on SQL Server, or [ConcurrencyCheck] int). On save, EF adds the value it originally read to the UPDATE's WHERE clause. If someone changed the row in the meantime, no row matches, and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException instead of overwriting.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- EF does not run a separate SELECT and retry; the check is inside the UPDATE itself, and retrying is your decision.
- SaveChanges takes no table lock; the conditional WHERE is optimistic.
- No trigger is involved, and a mismatch is an exception, not a silent overwrite with a warning.

This replaces the Java store's whole-file baseline compare.

excerpts.quote: EF issues `UPDATE ... WHERE Id = @p AND Version = @expected` and throws `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` when zero rows match

notes.title: One SaveChanges call already gives checkout its transaction
notes.body:
Checkout changes two rows: the book is updated and a loan is inserted. In EF Core both are tracked by one DbContext and written by a single SaveChangesAsync call. EF wraps that call in a transaction, so either both rows change or neither does, with no extra code.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Two SaveChangesAsync calls would need an explicit transaction to be atomic; the translation avoids that by using one call.
- No stored procedure is needed for a two-row change.
- Two contexts would split the change into two transactions, which is exactly what must not happen.

The Java version gets the same guarantee by committing one candidate snapshot.

excerpts.quote: a single `SaveChanges` call is already wrapped in a transaction, so either both rows change or neither does

notes.title: Archival in EF Core: a timestamp and a global filter
notes.body:
The tracker archives instead of deleting so loan history stays intact. In EF Core that becomes a nullable ArchivedAt column plus a global query filter that hides rows where ArchivedAt is set. The row stays in the table, so loans keep a valid foreign key to it.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Nothing later turns archival into a real delete; that would break the loans' history.
- The filter is global, registered once with HasQueryFilter, not repeated in every query by hand, and foreign keys are not nulled.
- Rows are not moved to another table, and no trigger re-points loans.

A global filter is easy to forget when you do need archived rows, so reports must opt out deliberately.

excerpts.quote: `ArchivedAt DateTime?` plus a global query filter `HasQueryFilter(b => b.ArchivedAt == null)`; loans keep their foreign key

notes.title: Importing ids into identity columns: map them, keep the source id
notes.body:
The Java store and SQL identity columns do not number records the same way, so the import cannot simply reuse old ids as new keys. The translation table's answer is to let the database assign new keys, keep a mapping from each source id to its new key while importing, and store the source id in its own column so every record can be traced back.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Reseeding identity to match the source is not what the table suggests.
- Dropping the ids and rebuilding references from titles and names would rely on display text, which is not identity.
- Turning identity generation off everywhere is not proposed either.

The separate source-id column also makes a re-run of the import detectable.

excerpts.quote: identity columns usually start at 1; the import path maps source ids to new keys and stores the source id in a separate column

notes.title: A CLI message that claims success the storage never delivered
notes.body:
The Entry Points checklist names three subtle bugs at the CLI. The one about messages is printing a result that sounds successful even though the save behind it failed. The user walks away believing the change is stored.

The other two subtle bugs are about input order (Scanner.nextLine() interactions are stateful) and formatting that assumes consistency the storage may not guarantee.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Localization is not discussed anywhere in the checklist.
- Duplicated success lines are not among its concerns.
- It does not ask for stack traces to be shown to users.

The matching review question is whether success and failure messages are still aligned with actual outcomes.

excerpts.quote: displaying a result that sounds successful even when persistence failed

notes.title: Why the last record of a file is where parsers slip
notes.body:
A simple line-oriented format depends on separators between records. If the file ends with an extra separator, or is missing the final one, the parser may read the last record differently from all the others, for example dropping it or merging it with garbage. The checklist lists this among the subtle persistence bugs, next to date parsing failures that break startup and clean-up logic that changes the durable format.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Byte-order marks are not mentioned.
- The checklist does not talk about header newlines.
- Buffer sizes and split reads are not among its concerns.

A save-then-load round trip is the natural test for this.

excerpts.quote: a trailing or missing record separator changing how the last record is parsed

notes.title: Hiding a menu option is not the same as protecting it
notes.body:
There is no authentication in this repo yet, so the checklist describes what to watch for when it arrives. Rules must be enforced in the service layer with one obvious enforcement point. The question that exposes a weak design is whether a restriction still holds when a caller bypasses the UI, and the junior trap is treating visibility as security: hiding a menu option while the service call stays open.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Checking roles in the service layer is what the checklist recommends, not the trap.
- It does not discuss logging denied attempts.
- Encrypting the data files is not part of this section.

excerpts.quote: if a caller bypasses the UI, does the restriction still hold
treating visibility as security

notes.title: Blank is not malformed, and missing is not malformed either
notes.body:
The Error Handling section lists two subtle bugs. First, treating a blank value and a malformed value as the same thing, although they usually need different messages and different handling. Second, handling a missing file gracefully while a malformed file still crashes or misbehaves.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Endless save retries are not mentioned.
- The checklist asks each layer to validate what it owns; it does not describe storage-only validation or date-range gaps as its listed bugs.
- Exit codes after a failed startup are not discussed in this section.

Its review questions ask what the user and the developer each see when something fails.

excerpts.quote: assuming blank values and malformed values are the same thing
handling missing files but not malformed files

notes.title: The four tests the checklist would add first
notes.body:
The checklist's tests section names four starting points, all aimed at the parts that are easiest to break and hardest to notice: checkout success and failure paths, return success and failure paths, a save followed by a load that must give back the same data, and overdue display with due-date handling.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Menu numbering, prompt wording, exit codes and banners are presentation details, not the listed priorities.
- Field validators such as email or ISBN checks are not on the list.
- Load, concurrency and disk-full tests are not mentioned.

Note that the checklist was written when the repo had no tests; the current repo has a test folder, so treat the list as priorities, not as a description of today's coverage.

excerpts.quote: `LibraryManager.checkOutBook` success and failure paths
`FileStorage.save` followed by `load` round-trip behavior

notes.title: Practice checks live outside the repo and drive the real CLI
notes.body:
The practice checks are plain node --test files with no dependencies, kept in a sibling folder such as ../j2-practice/ so the repo stays untouched. Each run, the shared helper compiles the Java sources into a fresh temporary folder and then feeds lines to the real CLI through stdin, exactly as a librarian would type them.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- They are not in the repo's test/ folder and do not call LibraryManager directly; they go through the CLI.
- Storage is not mocked; each check gets a fresh real data directory under the temp folder.
- Nothing is replayed without Java; every run compiles and starts the program.

Because of this, every check tests behaviour a user could actually see.

excerpts.quote: The shared helper compiles `src/` into the OS temp folder on every run (allow up to a minute), then drives the real CLI through stdin.

notes.title: Why some scenarios must be written straight to the snapshot file
notes.body:
To test anything about overdue loans you need a loan whose due date is already in the past. The CLI cannot produce one: checkout always uses today's clock, and the Book constructor refuses a due date before the checkout date. So the helper writes a valid LIBRARY2 snapshot file directly, and the program still validates that file when it starts.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Typing speed is not the reason; the scenarios are small.
- The CLI writes the same snapshot format, as exercise 4 shows by reading a snapshot the real CLI wrote.
- Validation is not skipped: LibraryData checks the planted file at startup like any other.

excerpts.quote: so no CLI script can create an overdue loan. The helper writes a valid `LIBRARY2` file instead; `LibraryData` still validates it at startup.

notes.title: One active loan per copy, enforced by a partial unique index
notes.body:
In the Java store, LibraryData's constructor refuses two active loans for the same book. In SQL, exercise 4 moves that rule into the schema: a unique index on loans(book_id) that only covers rows where returned_at is null. Any number of returned loans may exist for a copy, but at most one open one.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- A plain unique index on book_id would forbid a copy from ever being lent twice.
- A CHECK constraint cannot count rows in another table.
- A trigger that deletes older loans would destroy history instead of refusing the second loan.

The same sketch keeps book_title and borrower_name on each loans row as accepted text.

excerpts.quote: a partial unique index on `loans(book_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL` replaces the "one active loan per copy" check

notes.title: What Base64 protects in the snapshot, and what it does not
notes.body:
Text fields are Base64-encoded in the snapshot so characters like | and = and non-ASCII letters cannot break the row format. A real TAB is different: it never reaches the file, because Values.text rejects ISO control characters and the CLI answers Change not accepted.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Base64 would encode a TAB safely, but the TAB is refused before encoding ever happens.
- Nothing replaces it with a space, and Base64 is used for all the text fields, not only ISBN and email.
- The TAB never gets into the row, so it cannot split it.

So the protection against control characters is validation, not encoding.

excerpts.quote: `Values.text` rejects ISO control characters, so the CLI answers `Change not accepted`. Base64 protects `|`, `=`, and non-ASCII text, not control characters.
